title: Proof
body_md:
Write $z=x+iy$. The series
\[
 E_\alpha(z;a,b)=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb Z}
 e^{-\pi |mz-n|^2/y}
 \bigl[1+\alpha\cos\bigl(2\pi(ma+nb)\bigr)\bigr]
\]
converges absolutely, since $|1+\alpha\cos t|\leq1+|\alpha|$.
Using
\[
 \operatorname{Im}(-1/z)=\frac{y}{|z|^2},\qquad
 \frac{|m(-1/z)-n|^2}{\operatorname{Im}(-1/z)}=\frac{|nz+m|^2}{y},\qquad
 |m(-\bar z)-n|^2=|mz+n|^2,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_\alpha(z+1;a-b,b)
 &=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi |mz-(n-m)|^2/y}
   \bigl[1+\alpha\cos\bigl(2\pi(ma+(n-m)b)\bigr)\bigr]\\
 &\overset{k=n-m}{=}E_\alpha(z;a,b),\\[4pt]
 E_\alpha(-1/z;-b,a)
 &=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi |nz+m|^2/y}
   \bigl[1+\alpha\cos\bigl(2\pi(na-mb)\bigr)\bigr]\\
 &\overset{(p,q)=(n,-m)}{=}E_\alpha(z;a,b),\\[4pt]
 E_\alpha(-\bar z;a,-b)
 &=\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi |mz+n|^2/y}
   \bigl[1+\alpha\cos\bigl(2\pi(ma-nb)\bigr)\bigr]\\
 &\overset{k=-n}{=}E_\alpha(z;a,b).
\end{aligned}
\]
The three changes of indices are bijections of $\mathbb Z^2$;
this proves \eqref{Eq21}. They also give the corresponding
invariances of $\theta(s;z)$ for every $s>0$.

For $p,q\in\mathbb Z$, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \cos\bigl(2\pi(m(a+p)+n(b+q))\bigr)
 &=\cos\bigl(2\pi(ma+nb)\bigr),\\
 \cos\bigl(2\pi(m(1-a)+n(1-b))\bigr)
 &=\cos\bigl(2\pi(m+n)-2\pi(ma+nb)\bigr)\\
 &=\cos\bigl(2\pi(ma+nb)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
These identities prove \eqref{Eq22} term by term.

The fundamental-domain property of \eqref{Fd3} and
\eqref{Eq21}--\eqref{Eq22} imply
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \forall\,(z;a,b)\in\mathbb H\times\mathbb R^2,\quad
 \exists\,(z';a',b')\in
 \overline{\mathcal D_{\mathcal G}}\times[0,1]^2:\\
 E_\alpha(z';a',b')=E_\alpha(z;a,b).
\end{gathered}
\]
Hence the three infima agree for every real $\alpha$, and the
minima agree whenever attained. For $0\leq\alpha\leq1$,
attainment follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cusp}.

body_md:
\label{lem:cusp}
For every $0\leq\alpha\leq1$, the unrestricted minimum of $E_\alpha$ is

head: environment
name: Compactness of the minimization problem

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{Prop21}, it suffices to consider
$z\in\overline{\mathcal D_{\mathcal G}}$ and $(a,b)\in[0,1]^2$.
For $t>0$ and $u\in\mathbb R$, the Jacobi product gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \vartheta(t;u)
 &=\prod_{k\geq1}(1-e^{-2\pi kt})
 \bigl[(1-e^{-\pi(2k-1)t})^2
       +4e^{-\pi(2k-1)t}\cos^2(\pi u)\bigr]\\
 &\geq\vartheta_4(t)>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Poisson summation and \eqref{eq:positive-translated} yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \theta(1;x+iy)
 &=\sqrt y\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi ym^2}\vartheta(y;mx)\\
 &\geq\sqrt y\,[\vartheta_3(y)+\vartheta_4(y)(\vartheta_3(y)-1)],\\
 J(x+iy;a,b)
 &=\sqrt y\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}
       \vartheta\bigl(y;a+x(n+b)\bigr)\\
 &\geq\sqrt y\,\vartheta_4(y)
       \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}
 =\frac1{\sqrt y}\vartheta(1/y;b)
 \geq\frac1{\sqrt y}\vartheta_4(1/y)=\vartheta_2(y).
\]
For $y\geq2$, the bounds
\[
 \vartheta_3(y)\geq1+2e^{-\pi y},\qquad
 \vartheta_4(y)\geq1-2e^{-\pi y}>0,\qquad
 \vartheta_2(y)\geq2e^{-\pi y/4}
\]
give
\[
 E_\alpha(x+iy;a,b)\geq
 \sqrt y\,[1+4e^{-\pi y}(1-e^{-\pi y})
               +2\alpha e^{-\pi y/4}(1-2e^{-\pi y})].
\]
Since
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac d{dy}\bigl[(2\pi y-1)e^{-\pi y}\bigr]
 &=\pi e^{-\pi y}(3-2\pi y)<0,\\
 \frac d{dy}\bigl[(\pi y-2)e^{-\pi y/4}\bigr]
 &=\frac\pi4e^{-\pi y/4}(6-\pi y)<0,
\end{aligned}
\]
we obtain, for $0\leq\alpha\leq1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &2\sqrt y\,\frac d{dy}
 \left\{\sqrt y\,[1+4e^{-\pi y}(1-e^{-\pi y})
                 +2\alpha e^{-\pi y/4}(1-2e^{-\pi y})]\right\}\\
 &\quad=1-4(2\pi y-1)e^{-\pi y}+4(4\pi y-1)e^{-2\pi y}\\
 &\qquad\quad-\alpha(\pi y-2)e^{-\pi y/4}
               +2\alpha(5\pi y-2)e^{-5\pi y/4}\\
 &\quad\geq1-4(2\pi y-1)e^{-\pi y}-(\pi y-2)e^{-\pi y/4}\\
 &\quad\geq1-4(4\pi-1)e^{-2\pi}-(2\pi-2)e^{-\pi/2}>\frac1{50}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the displayed lower bound is strictly increasing in $y$.
For $t>0$, the geometric and alternating series give
\[
 \vartheta_3(t)\leq1+\frac{2e^{-\pi t}}{1-e^{-3\pi t}},\qquad
 \vartheta_4(t)\leq1-2e^{-\pi t}+2e^{-4\pi t},\qquad
 \vartheta_2(t)\leq\frac{2e^{-\pi t/4}}{1-e^{-2\pi t}}.
\]
At the centered rectangular competitor, these imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \theta(1;i\sqrt3)
 &=3^{1/4}\vartheta_3(\sqrt3)^2
 <\frac{71}{50}<\sqrt2\,[1+4e^{-2\pi}(1-e^{-2\pi})],\\
 E_1(i\sqrt3;1/2,1/2)
 &=3^{1/4}\bigl[\vartheta_3(\sqrt3)^2
       +\vartheta_4(\sqrt3)\vartheta_2(\sqrt3)\bigr]\\
 &<\frac{201}{100}
 <\sqrt2\,[1+4e^{-2\pi}(1-e^{-2\pi})
                 +2e^{-\pi/2}(1-2e^{-2\pi})].
\end{aligned}
\]
Affine dependence on $\alpha$ therefore gives, for $y\geq2$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_\alpha(x+iy;a,b)
 &\geq\sqrt2\,[1+4e^{-2\pi}(1-e^{-2\pi})
                   +2\alpha e^{-\pi/2}(1-2e^{-2\pi})]\\
 &>(1-\alpha)\theta(1;i\sqrt3)
       +\alpha E_1(i\sqrt3;1/2,1/2)\\
 &=E_\alpha(i\sqrt3;1/2,1/2).
\end{aligned}
\]
The Gaussian series converge uniformly on
\[
 \{z\in\overline{\mathcal D_{\mathcal G}}:\operatorname{Im} z\leq2\}
 \times[0,1]^2.
\]
Continuity gives a minimum, and the strict comparison excludes $y\geq2$.

name: Elimination of the displacement

title: Proof
body_md:
With $u=2\pi a$ and $v=2\pi b$, the four retained pairs contribute
\[
 A\cos u+B\cos v+C\cos(u+v)+D\cos(u-v).
\]
For $t=\cos v$, minimization in $u$ gives precisely the minimum
in \eqref{eq:lower}. Every omitted coefficient of $E_\alpha$ is
$1+\alpha\cos(2\pi(ma+nb))\geq1-\alpha\geq0$.
Retaining the stated finite remainder proves the inequality.

Let $f(t)$ denote the function inside the minimum. The assumptions give
\[
 C/D=e^{4\pi x/y}\geq1,\qquad
 A(C+D)\geq2A\sqrt{CD}>4CD.
\]
If $x=0$, then $C=D$, $A>2C$, and $B>2C$. Thus
\[
 f(t)=(B-2C)t-A,\qquad t_0=-\frac{A}{2C}<-1,
\]
and the unique minimum is at $t=-1$, as asserted.
Assume henceforth that $C>D$. The radicand is positive for
$-1<t<1$, and
\[
 f''(t)=
 \frac{(C-D)^2(A^2-4CD)}
 {[A^2+(C-D)^2+2A(C+D)t+4CDt^2]^{3/2}}>0
 \qquad(-1<t<1).
\]
Thus $f$ is strictly convex on $[-1,1]$.
Solving $f'(t)=0$ on the branch containing $[-1,1]$ gives $t=t_0$.
Strict convexity then gives the unique constrained minimizer
$t=\max\{-1,\min\{1,t_0\}\}$.
The interior stationary value is
\[
 -\frac{A^2B^2+(C-D)^2(A^2+B^2-4CD)}
 {AB(C+D)+(C-D)\sqrt{(A^2-4CD)(B^2-4CD)}}.
\]
If $f'(-1)\geq0$, the minimum equals
$-B-|A-C-D|$. When the unconstrained stationary point lies outside
$[-1,1]$, its value is still a valid lower bound for the constrained
minimum; the projected point gives the exact value.
These formulas avoid cancellation as $D$ tends to zero.

At a minimizing $t$ for which
$A^2+(C-D)^2+2A(C+D)t+4CDt^2>0$, the corresponding cosines are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \cos u&=-\frac{A+(C+D)t}
 {\sqrt{A^2+(C-D)^2+2A(C+D)t+4CDt^2}},&\cos v&=t,\\
 \cos(u+v)&=\frac{-[A+(C+D)t]t-(C-D)(1-t^2)}
 {\sqrt{A^2+(C-D)^2+2A(C+D)t+4CDt^2}},\\
 \cos(u-v)&=\frac{-[A+(C+D)t]t+(C-D)(1-t^2)}
 {\sqrt{A^2+(C-D)^2+2A(C+D)t+4CDt^2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The shape derivative of the minimized contribution is obtained by
multiplying the derivatives of $A,B,C,D$ by
$2(1+\alpha\cos u)$ and the three analogous factors.
The finite remainder is differentiated termwise.

To justify the derivative bounds at changes of branch, the minimum is
taken over a compact displacement torus of smooth functions whose shape
derivatives are bounded on compact shape rectangles. It is therefore
locally Lipschitz. Along any line segment it is absolutely continuous,
and its derivative almost everywhere is bounded by the directional
derivatives at the minimizing displacements. The displayed cosine
formulas enclose those derivatives; when the radicand interval meets
zero, using $[-1,1]$ for every cosine remains valid.
Thus integrating the resulting derivative bounds along segments gives
rigorous shape-box estimates, including boxes meeting a branch change.

body_md:

For $7/40\leq\alpha\leq23/25$,
\[
 \min_{z\in\mathbb H,\ (a,b)\in\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2}
 E_\alpha(z;a,b)
 =\min_{z\in\mathbb H}E_\alpha(z;1/2,1/2).

configuration. In particular, the square lattice is the unique minimizing
shape for $2/5\leq\alpha\leq23/25$, modulo the stated symmetries.

label: lem:centerstrip
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:centerstrip}
For
\[
 0\leq x\leq\frac{39}{100},\qquad
 \frac{23}{25}\leq y\leq2,
\]
the unique minimum of $J(x+iy;\cdot,\cdot)$ is attained at
$(1/2,1/2)$ modulo integer translations.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
With $Q_{m,n}$ as in \eqref{eq:lattice-quadratic-form}, put
$u=2\pi(a-1/2)$ and $v=2\pi(b-1/2)$. Since
\[
 \cos\bigl(2\pi(ma+nb)\bigr)=(-1)^{m+n}\cos(mu+nv),
\]
we have the exact decomposition
\[
\begin{aligned}
 J(z;a,b)-J(z;1/2,1/2)
 ={}&\sum_{\substack{m,n\in\mathbb Z\\m+n\ \mathrm{odd}}}
 e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}\bigl[1-\cos(mu+nv)\bigr]\\
 &-\sum_{\substack{m,n\in\mathbb Z\\m+n\ \mathrm{even}}}
 e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}\bigl[1-\cos(mu+nv)\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
For integers $m,n$,
\[
 |e^{i(mu+nv)}-1|
 \leq|e^{imu}-1|+|e^{inv}-1|
 \leq |m|\,|e^{iu}-1|+|n|\,|e^{iv}-1|.
\]
Using $|e^{it}-1|^2=2(1-\cos t)$ gives
\[
 1-\cos(mu+nv)\leq
 \bigl(|m|\sqrt{1-\cos u}+|n|\sqrt{1-\cos v}\bigr)^2.
\]
Retaining $(m,n)=\pm(1,0),\pm(0,1)$ in the nonnegative odd sum
and applying this estimate to the even sum yields
\begin{align*}
 J(z;a,b)-J(z;1/2,1/2)\geq{}&
 \left(2e^{-\pi Q_{1,0}}-
 \sum_{\substack{m,n\in\mathbb Z\\m+n\ \mathrm{even}}}
 m^2e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}\right)(1-\cos u)\\
 &+\left(2e^{-\pi Q_{0,1}}-
 \sum_{\substack{m,n\in\mathbb Z\\m+n\ \mathrm{even}}}
 n^2e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}\right)(1-\cos v)\\
 &-2\left(\sum_{\substack{m,n\in\mathbb Z\\m+n\ \mathrm{even}}}
 |mn|e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}\right)
 \sqrt{(1-\cos u)(1-\cos v)}.
\end{align*}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-strip}, this quadratic form in
$\sqrt{1-\cos u}$ and $\sqrt{1-\cos v}$ is positive definite.
Hence the difference is strictly positive unless
\[
 \cos u=\cos v=1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (a,b)\equiv(1/2,1/2)\pmod{\mathbb Z^2}.
\]
Periodicity gives equality for these displacements.

label: lem:hex-shift-localization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hex-shift-localization}

$\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\le y\le \frac{\sqrt3}{2}+1/40$. Every global minimizer of $J(x+iy;\cdot)$

head: environment
name: Localization of the displacement

label: eq:hex-phasor
title: Proof
body_md:
With $A,B,C$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:four} and $Q_{m,n}$ as in
\eqref{eq:lattice-quadratic-form}, put
\[
 P=\sqrt{AB/C},\qquad Q=\sqrt{AC/B},\qquad R=\sqrt{BC/A}.
\]
For $U=2\pi a$ and $V=2\pi b$, define
\[
 \mathcal R(a,b)=
 \sum_{\substack{(m,n)\in\mathbb Z^2\\
 (m,n)\notin\{(0,0),\,\pm(1,0),\,\pm(0,1),\,\pm(1,1)\}}}
 e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}\cos(mU+nV).
\]
The exact decomposition is
\begin{align}
 J(x+iy;a,b)
 &=1+2\{A\cos U+B\cos V+C\cos(U+V)\}+\mathcal R(a,b)\\
 &=1-P^2-Q^2-R^2+|P+Qe^{iU}+Re^{-iV}|^2
       +\mathcal R(a,b).\label{eq:hex-phasor}
\end{align}
The strict triangle inequalities for $P,Q,R$, verified in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-localization}, imply that the last square vanishes
at exactly two points on the displacement torus.
Denote them by $\pm(a_0,b_0)$, choosing
$U_0=2\pi a_0$, $V_0=2\pi b_0$ in $(0,\pi)$. They are
determined by the exact identities
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-phasor-centers}
\begin{aligned}
 \cos U_0&=\frac{R^2-P^2-Q^2}{2A},&
 \cos V_0&=\frac{Q^2-P^2-R^2}{2B},\\
 \cos(U_0+V_0)&=\frac{P^2-Q^2-R^2}{2C}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the first two equations determine the angles in $(0,\pi)$;
the triangle identities give $Q\sin U_0=R\sin V_0$ and
$P+Q\cos U_0+R\cos V_0=0$.

For fixed $(x,y)$, set
\[
 \operatorname{osc}_{a,b}\mathcal R
 :=\max_{(a,b)\in[0,1]^2}\mathcal R(a,b)
   -\min_{(a,b)\in[0,1]^2}\mathcal R(a,b),
\]
\[
 \nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R=(\partial_a\mathcal R,\partial_b\mathcal R),
 \qquad
 \|\nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R\|_2
 :=\sqrt{|\partial_a\mathcal R|^2+|\partial_b\mathcal R|^2}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-localization} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-cap-tail}
 \operatorname{osc}_{a,b}\mathcal R<\frac{27}{100000},\qquad
 \sup_{(a,b)\in[0,1]^2}\|\nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R(a,b)\|_2<\frac1{625},
\end{equation}
together with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-cap-coarse}
\begin{gathered}
 A>\frac1{40},\quad B>\frac1{38},\quad C>\frac1{44},\qquad
 P<\frac{19}{100},\quad Q<\frac16,\quad R<\frac7{40},\\
 -\frac{16}{25}<\cos U_0<0,\qquad
 -\frac23<\cos V_0<0,\qquad \cos(U_0+V_0)<-\frac29.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-localization} establishes these bounds uniformly
on the cap. In particular, $U_0,V_0\in(\pi/2,3\pi/4)$.

Let $(a,b)$ minimize $J$ at the fixed shape. Its existence follows
from continuity on the compact torus. Comparison with $(a_0,b_0)$
and \eqref{eq:hex-phasor} gives
\[
 |P+Qe^{iU}+Re^{-iV}|^2
 \le\mathcal R(a_0,b_0)-\mathcal R(a,b)
 <\frac{27}{100000}.
\]
Hence
\[
 |P+Qe^{iU}+Re^{-iV}|<\sqrt{\frac{27}{100000}}<\frac{33}{2000}.
\]
The triangle inequality implies
$\big||P+Qe^{iU}|-R\big|<\frac{33}{2000}$; squaring and using
\eqref{eq:hex-phasor-centers} gives
\[
 |\cos U-\cos U_0|
 <\frac{33(2R+33/2000)}{4000A}.
\]
The other two pairings give, in the same way,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-angular-errors}
 \begin{aligned}
 |\cos V-\cos V_0|
 &<\frac{33(2Q+33/2000)}{4000B},\\
 |\cos(U+V)-\cos(U_0+V_0)|
 &<\frac{33(2P+33/2000)}{4000C}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The elementary inequalities
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\sqrt{369}}{25}\sin\frac{7\pi}{125}
 -\frac{16}{25}\left(1-\cos\frac{7\pi}{125}\right)
 &>\frac{33}{100}\left(\frac7{20}+\frac{33}{2000}\right),\\
 \frac{\sqrt5}{3}\sin\frac{27\pi}{500}
 -\frac23\left(1-\cos\frac{27\pi}{500}\right)
 &>\frac{627}{2000}\left(\frac13+\frac{33}{2000}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]
and monotonicity of cosine on $[0,\pi]$ imply
\[
 |a\mp a_0|<\frac7{250},\qquad |b\mp b_0|<\frac{27}{1000},
\]
with the signs initially chosen independently.

The last inequality in \eqref{eq:hex-angular-errors}, with
\eqref{eq:hex-cap-coarse}, gives
\[
 \cos(U+V)<-\frac29+\frac{363}{1000}
                   \left(\frac{19}{50}+\frac{33}{2000}\right)<0.
\]
If the
signs were opposite, the representative of $U+V$ closest to zero
would satisfy
\[
 |U+V|<\frac\pi4+2\pi\left(\frac7{250}+\frac{27}{1000}\right)
       =\frac{9\pi}{25}<\frac\pi2,
\]
because $U_0,V_0\in(\pi/2,3\pi/4)$. Its cosine would then be
positive, a contradiction. After simultaneous inversion, we may
therefore suppose that
\[
 |a-a_0|<\frac7{250},\qquad |b-b_0|<\frac{27}{1000}.
\]

The displacement Hessian satisfies the uniform estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-cap-shift-convexity}
 D^2_{a,b}J(x+iy;a,b)\ge\frac{13}{20}I_2
 \quad\text{when }|a-a_0|,|b-b_0|\le\frac3{100}.
\end{equation}
This is the displacement-Hessian assertion of
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-hessians}. Set $v=(a-a_0,b-b_0)^{\mathsf T}$.
The segment $(a_0,b_0)+tv$, $0\le t\le1$, lies in the displayed
rectangle. Since $\nabla_{a,b}J(a,b)=0$ and
$\nabla_{a,b}J(a_0,b_0)=\nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R(a_0,b_0)$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{13}{20}\|v\|_2^2
 &\le\int_0^1 v^{\mathsf T}
 D^2_{a,b}J\bigl((a_0,b_0)+tv\bigr)v\,dt\\
 &=-v\cdot\nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R(a_0,b_0)
 \le\|v\|_2\|\nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R(a_0,b_0)\|_2
 <\frac{\|v\|_2}{625}\qquad(v\ne0).
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-cap-shift-distance}
 \|(a,b)-(a_0,b_0)\|_2<\frac4{1625}.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-localization} also gives the affine enclosures
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-cap-affine-centers}
\begin{aligned}
 \left|a_0-\left\{\frac13-\left(x-\frac12\right)
                   -\frac{29}{50}\left(y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\right\}\right|
 &\le\frac1{200},\\
 \left|b_0-\left\{\frac13+\frac{29}{25}\left(y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\right\}\right|
 &\le\frac7{2000}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Combining
\eqref{eq:hex-cap-shift-distance} and
\eqref{eq:hex-cap-affine-centers} proves
\[
 |r_a|<\frac1{200}+\frac4{1625}<\frac3{400},\qquad
 |r_b|<\frac7{2000}+\frac4{1625}<\frac3{500}.
\]

label: lem:hex-convexity
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Positive definiteness of the joint Hessian

label: eq:hex-joint-hessian
title: Proof
body_md:
For $Q_{m,n}$ from \eqref{eq:lattice-quadratic-form}, the Hessian of
$e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}[1+\alpha\cos(2\pi(ma+nb))]$ has the following
blocks, corresponding to $(x,y)$ and $(a,b)$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-joint-hessian}
\begin{aligned}
 H_{11}&=e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}[1+\alpha\cos(2\pi(ma+nb))]\\
 &\qquad\times[\pi^2\nabla Q_{m,n}(\nabla Q_{m,n})^{\mathsf T}
                   -\pi D^2Q_{m,n}],\\
 H_{12}&=2\alpha\pi^2e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}
 \sin(2\pi(ma+nb))\nabla Q_{m,n}\begin{pmatrix}m&n\end{pmatrix},\\
 H_{22}&=-4\alpha\pi^2e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}
 \cos(2\pi(ma+nb))\begin{pmatrix}m^2&mn\\mn&n^2\end{pmatrix},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where the derivatives of $Q_{m,n}$ are taken in $(x,y)$:
\[
 \nabla Q_{m,n}=\left(\frac{2m(mx-n)}y,
                 m^2-\frac{(mx-n)^2}{y^2}\right)^{\mathsf T},
\]
\[
 D^2Q_{m,n}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 2m^2/y&-2m(mx-n)/y^2\\
 -2m(mx-n)/y^2&2(mx-n)^2/y^3
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The series of these Hessians converges uniformly on the prism;
the tail estimate is given in \eqref{eq:hex-joint-hessian-tail}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-hessians} proves the endpoint estimates.
On \eqref{eq:hex-affine-prism}, therefore,
\[
 D^2E_\alpha
 =\frac{7/40-\alpha}{7/40-4/25}D^2E_{4/25}
  +\frac{\alpha-4/25}{7/40-4/25}D^2E_{7/40}\succ0
 \qquad\left(\frac4{25}\le\alpha\le\frac7{40}\right).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\alpha\in[4/25,7/40]$, and regard $E_\alpha$ as a function
of the four real variables $(x,y,a,b)$.
It attains its minimum on the closed shape rectangle in the statement
times the displacement torus. Choose such a minimizing configuration
$p=(x,y,a,b)$. Since $\alpha>0$, its displacement minimizes $J$
at the fixed shape. Lemma~\ref{lem:hex-shift-localization} places
$p$, after simultaneous displacement inversion and integer
translations, in the affine prism \eqref{eq:hex-affine-prism}.
This prism is convex and contains
\[
 p_0=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac13,\frac13\right).
\]

The triangular configuration is stationary in all four variables.
Indeed, the joint modular symmetry and integer periodicity give
\[
 E_\alpha\circ\Phi=E_\alpha,\qquad
 \Phi(z;a,b)=\left(1-\frac1z;1-a-b,a\right),\qquad
 \Phi(p_0)=p_0.
\]
At $p_0$, the shape derivative is multiplication by
$e^{-2\pi i/3}$, and the displacement derivative is
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Thus $\det(I-D\Phi(p_0))=9$, and differentiation yields
\[
 (I-D\Phi(p_0)^{\mathsf T})\nabla E_\alpha(p_0)=0,
 \qquad \nabla E_\alpha(p_0)=0.
\]

Suppose that $p\ne p_0$. If the minimum is attained in the
interior of the shape rectangle, then $\nabla E_\alpha(p)=0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:hex-convexity} and integration give the contradiction
\[
\begin{aligned}
 0&=(p-p_0)\cdot[\nabla E_\alpha(p)-\nabla E_\alpha(p_0)]\\
 &=\int_0^1(p-p_0)^{\mathsf T}
 D^2E_\alpha(p_0+t(p-p_0))(p-p_0)\,dt>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
If $p$ lies on the shape boundary, convexity keeps
$p-s(p-p_0)$ feasible for $0\le s\le1$. Minimality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 0&\le\left.\frac d{ds}E_\alpha(p-s(p-p_0))\right|_{s=0^+}\\
 &=-\int_0^1(p-p_0)^{\mathsf T}
 D^2E_\alpha(p_0+t(p-p_0))(p-p_0)\,dt<0,
\end{aligned}
\]
again a contradiction. Every minimum is therefore the triangular
deep-hole configuration, up to inversion and integer translations.
The two deep holes have the same energy by inversion, proving the
comparison and all equality cases.

label: thm:large-alpha-unrestricted
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:large-alpha-unrestricted}
Let $8/15\leq\alpha\leq1$. After a change of lattice basis and reflection,
every global minimizer of $E_\alpha(z;a,b)$ has
\[
 z=iy,\quad y\geq1,\qquad (a,b)\equiv(1/2,1/2)\pmod{\mathbb Z^2}.
\]
The minimizing lattice is square for
$8/15\leq\alpha\leq\alpha_c$ and centered rectangular for
$\alpha_c<\alpha\leq1$, with the aspect ratio $y_\alpha$ defined in Section~\ref{sec:introduction}. At
$\alpha=1$ the aspect ratio is $\sqrt3$.
head: environment

label: lem:same-height
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:same-height}
Let $|x|\leq1/2$, $y\geq\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$, and $\alpha\geq8/15$. Then
\[
 E_\alpha(x+iy;a,b)\geq E_\alpha(iy;1/2,1/2).
\]
Equality holds exactly when $x=0$ and
$(a,b)\equiv(1/2,1/2)\pmod{\mathbb Z^2}$.
head: environment

label: eq:large-alpha-tails
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $y\geq\sqrt3/2$, we have $e^{-\pi y}<1/15$. The
alternating series and the estimates
$n^2\geq4+5(n-2)$, $n^2\leq4\,3^{n-2}$ for $n\geq2$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-alpha-tails}
 \vartheta_4(y)\geq1-2e^{-\pi y},\qquad
 \sum_{n\geq1}n^2e^{-\pi yn^2}
 \leq e^{-\pi y}(1+5e^{-3\pi y}).
\end{equation}
Indeed,
\[
 \sum_{n\geq2}n^2e^{-\pi yn^2}
 \leq\frac{4e^{-4\pi y}}{1-3e^{-5\pi y}}<5e^{-4\pi y}.
\]
The Jacobi product implies that $\vartheta(y;\cdot)$ has its
unique minimum $\vartheta_4(y)$ at $1/2$ modulo $\mathbb Z$.
More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quantified-one-d}
 \vartheta(y;t)\geq\vartheta_4(y)
 +4e^{-\pi y}(1-5e^{-3\pi y})\cos^2(\pi t).
\end{equation}
The $k=1$ pair contributes $4e^{-\pi y}\cos^2(\pi t)$ to the
difference. Every odd $k$ contributes a nonnegative quantity,
whereas for even $k$, $|\sin(ku)|\leq k|\sin u|$ bounds its
contribution below by
$-4k^2e^{-\pi yk^2}\cos^2(\pi t)$.
Thus \eqref{eq:large-alpha-tails} proves
\eqref{eq:quantified-one-d}.

Rowwise Poisson summation gives
\[
 \theta(1;x+iy)=\sqrt y\sum_{m,k\in\mathbb Z}
 e^{-\pi y(m^2+k^2)}\cos(2\pi mkx).
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:theta-shear-loss}
\begin{aligned}
 0\leq\theta(1;iy)-\theta(1;x+iy)
 &=8\sqrt y\sum_{m,k\geq1}
 e^{-\pi y(m^2+k^2)}\sin^2(\pi mkx)\\
 &\leq8\sqrt y\,e^{-2\pi y}(1+5e^{-3\pi y})^2
 \sin^2(\pi x).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The translated representation of $J$, followed by horizontal
Poisson summation, yields
\[
 J(x+iy;a,b)=\sqrt y\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}
 e^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}\vartheta\bigl(y;a+x(n+b)\bigr),
 \quad
 J(iy;1/2,1/2)=\sqrt y\,\vartheta_4(y)\vartheta_2(y).
\]
By periodicity, take $0\leq b\leq1$. The Jacobi product after
one-dimensional Poisson summation shows that
$\sum_ne^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}$ decreases strictly on $[0,1/2]$,
is symmetric about $1/2$, and has minimum $\vartheta_2(y)$.
Retaining the $n=0,-1$ corrections in
\eqref{eq:quantified-one-d} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-row-penalty}
\begin{aligned}
 &J(x+iy;a,b)-\sqrt y\,\vartheta_4(y)\vartheta_2(y)\\
 &\quad\geq\sqrt y\left[
 \vartheta_4(y)\left(\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}
 -\vartheta_2(y)\right)
 +\frac{4e^{-\pi y}(1-5e^{-3\pi y})}
 {e^{\pi yb^2}+e^{\pi y(1-b)^2}}\sin^2(\pi x)\right].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here, for $\lambda,\mu>0$,
\[
 \min_u\{\lambda\cos^2u+\mu\cos^2(u-\pi x)\}
 =\frac{\lambda+\mu-
 \sqrt{(\lambda+\mu)^2-4\lambda\mu\sin^2(\pi x)}}2
 \geq\frac{\lambda\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\sin^2(\pi x).
\]

Suppose first that $\sqrt3/2\leq y\leq1$. Since
$e^{-\pi/y}<1/23$, Poisson summation and
\eqref{eq:quantified-one-d}, applied at $1/y$, imply
\[
 \sum_ne^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}-\vartheta_2(y)
 \geq\frac{4e^{-\pi/y}(1-5e^{-3\pi/y})}{\sqrt y}
 \sin^2\bigl(\pi(b-1/2)\bigr).
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \frac1{e^{\pi yb^2}+e^{\pi y(1-b)^2}}
 =\frac{e^{-\pi y/4}}2
 \frac{e^{-\pi y(b-1/2)^2}}{\cosh\bigl(\pi y(b-1/2)\bigr)}
 \geq\frac{e^{-\pi y/4}}2
 \cos^2\bigl(\pi(b-1/2)\bigr).
\]
Indeed, $\log\cosh u\leq u^2/2$, $\log\cos u\leq-u^2/2$
for $|u|<\pi/2$, and
$\pi y+\pi^2y^2/2\leq\pi+\pi^2/2<\pi^2$; the endpoints
follow by continuity. Also,
\[
 \frac{4\vartheta_4(y)e^{-\pi/y}(1-5e^{-3\pi/y})}{\sqrt y}
 >2e^{-5\pi y/4}(1-5e^{-3\pi y}),
\]
because
\[
 e^{-\pi(5y/4-1/y)}
 \leq e^{\pi/(8\sqrt3)}<\frac43
 <\frac53<2\frac{13}{15}\left(1-\frac5{23^3}\right).
\]
Inserting these inequalities into \eqref{eq:two-row-penalty} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-height-penalty}
 J(x+iy;a,b)-\sqrt y\,\vartheta_4(y)\vartheta_2(y)
 \geq2\sqrt y\,e^{-5\pi y/4}(1-5e^{-3\pi y})\sin^2(\pi x).
\end{equation}
The ratio of the bound in \eqref{eq:theta-shear-loss} to that in
\eqref{eq:low-height-penalty} is at most
\[
 4e^{-3\pi y/4}\frac{(1+5e^{-3\pi y})^2}{1-5e^{-3\pi y}}
 <4\,15^{-3/4}\frac{(1+5/15^3)^2}{1-5/15^3}<\frac8{15}.
\]
This proves the comparison in this height range, strictly if $x\ne0$.

Now let $y\geq1$, so $e^{-\pi y}<1/23$. For
$1/3\leq b\leq2/3$, convexity and symmetry about $1/2$ yield
\[
 \frac1{e^{\pi yb^2}+e^{\pi y(1-b)^2}}
 \geq\frac{e^{-4\pi y/9}}{1+e^{-\pi y/3}}.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:two-row-penalty} implies
\[
 J(x+iy;a,b)-\sqrt y\,\vartheta_4(y)\vartheta_2(y)
 \geq\frac{4\sqrt y\,e^{-13\pi y/9}(1-5e^{-3\pi y})}
 {1+e^{-\pi y/3}}\sin^2(\pi x).
\]
The ratio of the theta loss to this bound satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-alpha-interior-bound}
\begin{aligned}
 2e^{-5\pi y/9}(1+e^{-\pi y/3})
 \frac{(1+5e^{-3\pi y})^2}{1-5e^{-3\pi y}}
 &<2\,23^{-5/9}(1+23^{-1/3})
 \frac{(1+5/23^3)^2}{1-5/23^3}
 \\
 &<\frac12<\frac8{15}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The desired comparison is therefore strict if $x\ne0$.

If $b\notin[1/3,2/3]$, monotonicity gives
\[
 \sum_ne^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}-\vartheta_2(y)
 \geq e^{-\pi y/9}+e^{-4\pi y/9}+e^{-16\pi y/9}
 -\frac{2e^{-\pi y/4}}{1-e^{-2\pi y}}.
\]
Here we retained three positive terms in the first series and used
$(n+1/2)^2\geq1/4+2n$ in the second. For
$y\geq(\log23)/\pi$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\frac{36e^{-5\pi y/36}}{\pi}\frac d{dy}
 \left(e^{5\pi y/36}+e^{-7\pi y/36}+e^{-55\pi y/36}
 -\frac2{1-e^{-2\pi y}}\right)\\
 &\qquad\geq5-7e^{-\pi y/3}-55e^{-5\pi y/3}>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 e^{5\pi y/36}+e^{-7\pi y/36}+e^{-55\pi y/36}
 -\frac2{1-e^{-2\pi y}}
 &\geq23^{5/36}+23^{-7/36}+23^{-55/36}
 -\frac2{1-23^{-2}}\\
 &>\frac9{100}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
 J(x+iy;a,b)-\sqrt y\,\vartheta_4(y)\vartheta_2(y)
 >\frac9{100}\sqrt y\,(1-2e^{-\pi y})e^{-\pi y/4}.
\]
This penalty dominates the theta loss divided by $\alpha$, since
\[
 \frac{8e^{-7\pi y/4}(1+5e^{-3\pi y})^2}
 {(9/100)(1-2e^{-\pi y})}
 <\frac{8\,23^{-7/4}(1+5/23^3)^2}{(9/100)(1-2/23)}
 <\frac12<\frac8{15}.
\]
The comparison is strict throughout this range of $b$.

Finally, at $x=0$ the theta functions agree, while
\[
 J(iy;a,b)=\sqrt y\,\vartheta(y;a)
 \sum_ne^{-\pi y(n+b)^2}.
\]
The unique minima of its two positive factors require
$a\equiv b\equiv1/2\pmod{\mathbb Z}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Modular reduction places every candidate in
$|x|\leq1/2$, $|z|\geq1$, hence $y\geq\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:same-height} forces every minimizer to be centered
rectangular; the reduced-domain condition then gives $y\geq1$.

head: environment

label: eq:crossing-endpoint-signs
title: Proof
body_md:
At $\alpha=0$, the centered classification gives
\[
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_0(\tau;1/2,1/2)
 =E_0(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)=\theta(1;e^{i\pi/3}).
\]
The centered minimum is continuous on $[0,1]$. The difference
\[
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_\alpha(\tau;1/2,1/2)
       -E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
\]
is concave: its first term is the infimum of affine functions of
$\alpha$, and its second term is affine.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-thresholds} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-endpoint-signs}
\begin{aligned}
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_{1723/10000}(\tau;1/2,1/2)
 -E_{1723/10000}(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
     &>0,\\
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_{7/40}(\tau;1/2,1/2)
 -E_{7/40}(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
     &<0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Concavity and the first inequality in
\eqref{eq:crossing-endpoint-signs} imply
\[
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_\alpha(\tau;1/2,1/2)
 >E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
 \qquad(0<\alpha\leq1723/10000).
\]
Continuity and the second inequality give a zero of the energy
difference between $1723/10000$ and $7/40$. The secant slope from
$1723/10000$ to any subsequent zero is strictly negative. Concavity
makes the difference strictly negative beyond that zero, proving
uniqueness of $\alpha_a$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-signs}
\begin{aligned}
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_\alpha(\tau;1/2,1/2)
     &>E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
                        &&(0<\alpha<\alpha_a),\\
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_\alpha(\tau;1/2,1/2)
     &<E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
                        &&(\alpha_a<\alpha\leq1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Throughout the initial bracket the centered minimizer is rhombic.
At the crossing, put $x_*:=\cos\varphi_{\alpha_a}$.
Its stationarity and energy equality give, with $z=x+i\sqrt{1-x^2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-system}
\begin{aligned}
 E_\alpha(z;1/2,1/2)&=E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3),\\
 \frac{d}{dx}E_\alpha(z;1/2,1/2)&=0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Conversely, a
solution of that system on the centered minimizing branch gives a
zero of the energy difference, and hence must have coupling $\alpha_a$.
Uniqueness of the centered minimizer then also determines $x_*$.

Eliminating $\alpha$ from \eqref{eq:crossing-system} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-residual}
 \bigl(\theta(1;z)-\theta(1;e^{i\pi/3})\bigr)
       \frac{d}{dx}J(z;1/2,1/2)
 -\frac{d}{dx}\theta(1;z)
       \bigl(J(z;1/2,1/2)-J(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)\bigr)=0.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-thresholds} supplies a sign-changing interval
for \eqref{eq:crossing-residual}, on which the derivative quotient satisfies
\[
 -\frac{\frac{d}{dx}\theta(1;x+i\sqrt{1-x^2})}
        {\frac{d}{dx}J(x+i\sqrt{1-x^2};1/2,1/2)}
 \in\left(\frac{1723}{10000},\frac7{40}\right).
\]
The intermediate value theorem gives a zero. The centered
classification identifies its quotient with a minimizing coupling;
the single-crossing argument then identifies the pair with
$(x_*,\alpha_a)$.
The energy equality yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:crossing-quotient}
 \alpha_a=
 \frac{\theta(1;x_*+i\sqrt{1-x_*^2})-\theta(1;e^{i\pi/3})}
 {J(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)-J(x_*+i\sqrt{1-x_*^2};1/2,1/2)}.
\end{equation}
The denominator is strictly positive, since $\alpha_a>0$ and the
unshifted theta difference is strictly positive at the nontriangular
shape $x_*+i\sqrt{1-x_*^2}$.

name: Proof of the threshold characterization

label: lem:first-transition
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:first-transition}
For $1723/10000\leq\alpha\leq7/40$, every shape and displacement satisfy
\[
 E_\alpha(z;a,b)\geq
 \min\left\{E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3),\,
       \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_\alpha(\tau;1/2,1/2)\right\}.
\]
Equality holds precisely at the triangular deep holes for
$\alpha<\alpha_a$, at the centered rhombic minimizer for
$\alpha>\alpha_a$, and at both families for $\alpha=\alpha_a$.
In the last case,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:supporting-inequality}
 E_{\alpha_a}(z;a,b)\geq E_{\alpha_a}(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)=\min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_{\alpha_a}(\tau;1/2,1/2),
\end{equation}
All equality statements are understood modulo the stated symmetries.
head: environment
name: Comparison across the first transition

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:cusp}, an unrestricted minimizer has a reduced
representative with $y<2$. We compare its energy with the smaller
of the two values in the statement.

If $x\leq39/100$, then
$y\geq\sqrt{1-(39/100)^2}>23/25$, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:centerstrip} gives
\[
 E_\alpha(z;a,b)\geq E_\alpha(z;1/2,1/2)
 \geq\min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_\alpha(\tau;1/2,1/2).
\]
Equality in both inequalities requires the centered displacement and,
by the centered classification, the rhombic minimizing shape.
For $x\geq39/100$, Proposition~\ref{prop:bridge} strictly excludes
every shape outside
\[
 \frac{19}{40}\leq x\leq\frac12,\qquad
 \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\leq y\leq\frac{891}{1000},
\]
since its centered competitor has energy at least the centered minimum.
This remaining cap is contained in the region of
Theorem~\ref{cor:hex-cap-comparison}, because
$891/1000<\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+1/40$. Hence
\[
 E_\alpha(z;a,b)\geq E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3),
\]
with equality precisely at the triangular deep-hole configurations.
The unrestricted minimum is therefore at least the smaller of the
two stated energies. Both energies are attained by admissible
configurations, so this lower bound is the unrestricted minimum.
The inequality consequently holds for every shape and displacement.
Finally, \eqref{eq:crossing-signs} and equality at $\alpha_a$ give
the asserted equality configurations on each side of the transition
and at the transition itself.
head: environment

label: eq:coupling-interpolation
title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:first-transition} and
$\frac{1723}{10000}<\alpha_a$ give
\[
 E_{1723/10000}(z;a,b)\geq E_{1723/10000}(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3),
\]
with equality precisely at the triangular deep-hole configurations.
For $0<\alpha<\frac{1723}{10000}$, affine dependence gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coupling-interpolation}
\begin{aligned}
 &E_\alpha(z;a,b)-E_\alpha(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)\\
 &\quad=\left(1-\frac{10000\alpha}{1723}\right)
       \bigl[\theta(1;z)-\theta(1;e^{i\pi/3})\bigr]\\
 &\qquad+\frac{10000\alpha}{1723}
       \bigl[E_{1723/10000}(z;a,b)-E_{1723/10000}(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)\bigr]
       \geq0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Both coefficients are strictly positive, and both bracketed differences
are nonnegative by Montgomery's theorem and the comparison at $\frac{1723}{10000}$.
Equality forces the triangular deep-hole configurations. Thus the
entire interval $0<\alpha<\frac{1723}{10000}$ follows from a single comparison
at a rational coupling.

The remaining comparisons cover
\[
 [\frac{1723}{10000},7/40]\cup[7/40,8/15]\cup[8/15,1]=[\frac{1723}{10000},1].
\]
On $[\frac{1723}{10000},7/40]$, Lemma~\ref{lem:first-transition} and
\eqref{eq:crossing-signs} give the triangular phase up to $\alpha_a$,
both minimizing families at $\alpha_a$, and the centered rhombic
phase above it. We use Theorem~\ref{thm:centered} only on
$[7/40,8/15]$, which is contained in its stated range, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:large-alpha-unrestricted} on $[8/15,1]$.
Every minimizer for $\alpha>\alpha_a$ is therefore centered.
The classification of \cite[Theorem~2.1]{LW} gives the
rhombic, square, and rectangular phases, their transition endpoints,
and $y_1=\sqrt3$. This completes the positive-coupling classification.
At $\alpha=0$, Montgomery's theorem fixes the triangular shape,
while $E_0=\theta(1;z)$ is independent of displacement.

For completeness, Lemma~\ref{lem:analytic-properties} also gives
the nonpositive-coupling cases. For $-1<\alpha<0$,
\[
 E_\alpha(z;a,b)\geq(1+\alpha)\theta(1;z)
 \geq(1+\alpha)\theta(1;e^{i\pi/3}),
\]
with equality exactly for a triangular lattice and coincident
displacement. At $\alpha=-1$, the energy is $\theta(1;z)-J(z;a,b)$,
so every coincident configuration minimizes, and these are the only
equality configurations.

label: lem:cert-strip
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cert-strip}
With $A,B$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:four} and $Q_{m,n}$ as in
\eqref{eq:lattice-quadratic-form}, define
\[
 H(x,y)=2\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&B\end{pmatrix}
 -\sum_{\substack{m,n\in\mathbb Z\\m+n\ \mathrm{even}}}
 e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}\begin{pmatrix}m^2&|mn|\\|mn|&n^2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If $0\leq x\leq39/100$ and $23/25\leq y\leq2$, then
\[
 H_{11}>\frac3{5000},\qquad H_{22}>\frac{17}{500},\qquad
 \det H>\frac1{10000},\qquad H\succ0.
\]
head: environment
name: Centered-strip estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
The determinant-one matrix of $Q_{m,n}$ has trace satisfying
\[
 y+\frac{1+x^2}{y}
 \le\frac{51521}{20000}<\frac{47}{100}+\frac{100}{47}.
\]
Hence $Q_{m,n}\ge(47/100)(m^2+n^2)$. Each omitted weighted
sum is bounded by
\[
 8\sum_{r\ge5}r^3e^{-47\pi r^2/100}<2\cdot10^{-12}.
\]
Use the $64$ rectangles
\[
 K_{jk}=\left[\frac{39j}{400},\frac{39(j+1)}{400}\right]
 \times\left[\frac{368+27k}{400},\frac{395+27k}{400}\right],
 \quad0\le j<4,\quad0\le k<16.
\]
Let $\Lambda_4$ contain the pairs $0\le m\le4$, $|n|\le4$,
$m+n$ even, with $m>0$ or $n>0$. On each $K=K_{jk}$, set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 u_K&=\sum_{\substack{(m,n)\in\Lambda_4\\m\ne0}}
 m^2e^{-\pi\inf_K(Q_{m,n}-Q_{1,0})}+\frac{10^{-12}}{\inf_KA},\\
 v_K&=\sum_{\substack{(m,n)\in\Lambda_4\\n\ne0}}
 n^2e^{-\pi\inf_K(Q_{m,n}-Q_{0,1})}+\frac{10^{-12}}{\inf_KB},\\
 w_K&=\sum_{\substack{(m,n)\in\Lambda_4\\mn\ne0}}|mn|
 e^{-\pi\inf_K\{Q_{m,n}-(Q_{1,0}+Q_{0,1})/2\}}
 +\frac{10^{-12}}{\sqrt{(\inf_KA)(\inf_KB)}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All infima here have the form
$\inf_K\{ay+(ux^2-2vx+w)/y\}$, with $a,u\ge0$:
minimize the quadratic over the $x$ interval, then test the two
$y$ endpoints and $\sqrt{(ux^2-2vx+w)/a}$ when it belongs to
the $y$ interval and its numerator and $a$ are positive. Convexity gives $\inf_K A$ and $\inf_K B$
from the corner maxima of their exponents. The resulting finite
inequalities on every $K$ are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 2(\inf_KA)(1-u_K)&>\frac3{5000},\\
 2(\inf_KB)(1-v_K)&>\frac{17}{500},\\
 4(\inf_KA)(\inf_KB)\{(1-u_K)(1-v_K)-w_K^2\}
 &>\frac1{10000}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These bound $H_{11}$, $H_{22}$, and $\det H$, respectively.
Sylvester's criterion completes the proof.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cert-global}
Let
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2,\mathcal I_3)&=([7/40,9/50],\,[9/50,1/5],\,[1/5,6/25]),\\
 (\mathcal I_4,\mathcal I_5,\mathcal I_6)&=([6/25,3/10],\,[3/10,37/100],\,[37/100,2/5]),\\
 (t_1,\ldots,t_6)&=(371/1000,\,9/25,\,33/100,\,27/100,\,17/100,\,0),
\end{aligned}
\]
and put $z_j=t_j+i\sqrt{1-t_j^2}$. For $1\leq j\leq6$,
$\alpha\in \mathcal I_j$, every reduced shape with $39/100\leq x\leq1/2$,
$y\leq2$, and every displacement satisfy
\[
 E_\alpha(x+iy;a,b)-E_\alpha(z_j;1/2,1/2)>3\cdot10^{-8}.
\]
For $2/5\leq\alpha\leq23/25$, every reduced shape with
$3/10\leq x\leq1/2$, $y\leq2$, and every displacement satisfy
\[
 E_\alpha(x+iy;a,b)-E_\alpha(i;1/2,1/2)>5\cdot10^{-6}.
\]
For $1723/10000\leq\alpha\leq7/40$, the energy difference
\[
 E_\alpha(x+iy;a,b)
 -E_\alpha\left(\frac{3+i\sqrt{55}}8;\frac12,\frac12\right)
\]
is greater than $1.9\cdot10^{-8}$ when
$39/100\leq x\leq19/40$, $y\leq2$, and greater than
$2.4\cdot10^{-8}$ when $19/40\leq x\leq1/2$,
$891/1000\leq y\leq2$, for every reduced shape in the
indicated regions and every displacement.
head: environment
name: Energy comparisons

label: eq:energy-box-test
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f_\alpha$ be the lower bound in \eqref{eq:lower}; for the
square comparison omit its finite remainder. For a rectangle
$K=[x_-,x_+]\times[y_-,y_+]$, first discard it if
$x_+^2+y_+^2<1$, and otherwise replace $y_-$ by
$\max\{y_-,\sqrt{1-x_+^2}\}$. The clipped rectangle contains
$K\cap\{x^2+y^2\ge1\}$. Convexity gives
\[
 c^-_{m,n}(K)=\exp\!\left[-\pi
 \max_{\substack{x\in\{x_-,x_+\}\\y\in\{y_-,y_+\}}}Q_{m,n}(x,y)\right].
\]
The retained energy is increasing in every coefficient, since
$1+\alpha\cos(2\pi(ma+nb))\ge0$. Substitution of the
$c^-_{m,n}(K)$ in \eqref{eq:lower} therefore gives a lower bound
$L_\alpha(K)$ for $f_\alpha$. Lemma~\ref{lem:four} also gives
\[
 M_\alpha(K)=\underline{f_\alpha(x_c,y_c)}
 -r_x\sup_K|\partial_xf_\alpha|-r_y\sup_K|\partial_yf_\alpha|
 \le\inf_Kf_\alpha,
\]
where $(x_c,y_c)$ and $(r_x,r_y)$ are its center and half-widths.
The local Lipschitz property justifies this estimate across branch
changes. A test is omitted if its coefficient, denominator, or
radicand conditions are not yet verified.

At each coupling endpoint, start with
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 [39/100,1/2]\times[43/50,2]&\text{for the six arc comparisons},\\
 {}[3/10,1/2]\times[43/50,2]&\text{for the square comparison},\\
 {}[39/100,19/40]\times[43/50,2]&\text{for the first bridge},\\
 {}[19/40,1/2]\times[891/1000,2]&\text{for the second bridge}.
\end{array}
\]
Accept a clipped rectangle precisely when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:energy-box-test}
 \max\{L_\alpha(K),M_\alpha(K)\}
 -\overline{E_\alpha(z_t;1/2,1/2)}>\delta,
 \qquad z_t=t+i\sqrt{1-t^2},
\end{equation}
where $\delta$ is the asserted gap. Bisect each remaining rectangle
along its longer side, taking the $x$ side in a tie, and repeat.
The tests terminate by depth $15$. In the four groups above, the
smallest accepted lower bounds exceed, respectively,
\[
 \frac1{4000000},\qquad\frac7{125000},\qquad
 \frac{11}{5000000},\qquad\frac{11}{10000000}.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:energy-box-test} holds on a finite cover of each
reduced region. Only $|m|,|n|\le2$ are retained in the positive
remainder of \eqref{eq:lower}; all omitted terms are nonnegative.
The competitor upper bounds use $\theta_4+\alpha J_4$ and
\[
 16\sum_{r\ge5}re^{-9\pi r^2/10}<10^{-27},
\]
since the competitor heights exceed $9/10$ and
$Q_{m,n}\ge y\max(m^2,n^2)$ on their unit-circle shapes.
Finally, the energy difference from a fixed competitor is affine in
$\alpha$. Its endpoint bounds imply each assertion on the entire
coupling interval.

label: lem:cert-localization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cert-localization}
Let $19/40\leq x\leq1/2$ and
$0\leq y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\leq1/40$. Then the coefficient bounds
\eqref{eq:hex-cap-coarse} and the affine enclosures
\eqref{eq:hex-cap-affine-centers} hold, and
\[
 \operatorname{osc}_{a,b}\mathcal R<\frac{131}{500000},\qquad
 \sup_{(a,b)\in[0,1]^2}\|\nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R(a,b)\|_2
 <\frac{39}{25000}.
\]
head: environment
name: Displacement localization

label: eq:localization-cover
title: Proof
body_md:
The phasor lengths $P,Q,R$ defined in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:hex-shift-localization} have the exact expressions
\[
 P=e^{-\pi x/y},\qquad
 Q=e^{-\pi\{y+(x^2-x)/y\}},\qquad R=e^{-\pi(1-x)/y}.
\]
Corner bounds and one-variable extrema prove the coefficient
bounds in \eqref{eq:hex-cap-coarse}. For its cosine bounds, use
\eqref{eq:hex-phasor-centers} on the rectangles
\begin{equation}\label{eq:localization-cover}
 K_{jk}=\left[\frac{19}{40}+\frac j{1280},
                 \frac{19}{40}+\frac{j+1}{1280}\right]
 \times\left[\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac k{1280},
                 \frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{k+1}{1280}\right],
 \quad0\le j,k<32.
\end{equation}
The first two cosine ranges lie in $(-1,1)$, which also proves
the strict triangle inequalities.

Let $\Lambda'_4$ consist of $0\le m\le4$, $|n|\le4$,
$m>0$ or $n>0$, with $(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ removed.
The determinant-one quadratic form has trace less than $231/100$;
thus $Q_{m,n}\ge(57/100)(m^2+n^2)$. Bisecting both cap intervals
once gives four rectangles $K$. On each of them,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{osc}_{a,b}\mathcal R
 &\le4\sum_{(m,n)\in\Lambda'_4}e^{-\pi\inf_KQ_{m,n}}
       +2\cdot10^{-16}<\frac{131}{500000},\\
 \sup_{a,b}\|\nabla_{a,b}\mathcal R\|_2
 &\le4\pi\sum_{(m,n)\in\Lambda'_4}\sqrt{m^2+n^2}
        e^{-\pi\inf_KQ_{m,n}}+2\cdot10^{-14}<\frac{39}{25000}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two error terms follow from \eqref{eq:common-ring-tail} with
$(c,k)=(57/100,1)$ and $(57/100,2)$. The infima are evaluated
as in Lemma~\ref{lem:cert-strip}.

For the affine enclosures, apply the box mean-value estimate on
\eqref{eq:localization-cover} to
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F_1&=\cos\!\left(2\pi\left[\frac13-\left(x-\frac12\right)
 -\frac{29}{50}\left(y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-\frac1{200}\right]\right)-\cos U_0,\\
 F_2&=\cos U_0-\cos\!\left(2\pi\left[\frac13-\left(x-\frac12\right)
 -\frac{29}{50}\left(y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)+\frac1{200}\right]\right),\\
 F_3&=\cos\!\left(2\pi\left[\frac13+\frac{29}{25}
 \left(y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)-\frac7{2000}\right]\right)-\cos V_0,\\
 F_4&=\cos V_0-\cos\!\left(2\pi\left[\frac13+\frac{29}{25}
 \left(y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)+\frac7{2000}\right]\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The finite inequalities on every rectangle, with center $c_K$, are
\[
 \underline{F_i(c_K)}-\frac1{2560}
   \bigl(\sup_K|\partial_xF_i|+\sup_K|\partial_yF_i|\bigr)
 >\frac1{20000},\qquad1\le i\le4.
\]
All four affine endpoints lie in $(0,1/2)$. Monotonicity of cosine
on $[0,\pi]$ proves \eqref{eq:hex-cap-affine-centers}.

label: lem:cert-hessians
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cert-hessians}
Throughout $19/40\leq x\leq1/2$,
$0\leq y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\leq1/40$,
\[
 D^2_{a,b}J(x+iy;a,b)\geq\frac{13}{20}I_2
 \qquad\text{if }|a-a_0|,|b-b_0|\leq\frac3{100}.
\]
The full Hessian of $E_\alpha$ in $(x,y,a,b)$ is positive definite at
$\alpha=4/25$ on the affine prism
\eqref{eq:hex-affine-prism} enlarged to
$|r_a|,|r_b|\leq1/100$, and at $\alpha=7/40$ on
\eqref{eq:hex-affine-prism} itself.
head: environment
name: Hessian estimates

label: eq:hex-joint-hessian-tail
title: Proof
body_md:
The displacement Hessian is
\[
 D^2_{a,b}J=-4\pi^2\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb Z}e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}
 \cos\bigl(2\pi(ma+nb)\bigr)
 \begin{pmatrix}m^2&mn\\mn&n^2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For the joint Hessian use \eqref{eq:hex-joint-hessian}.
On the rational outer shape rectangle
\[
 \frac{4749}{10000}\le x\le\frac{5001}{10000},\qquad
 \frac{433}{500}\le y\le\frac{8911}{10000},
\]
completing the square gives $Q_{m,n}\ge(17/20)r^2$.
The first and second shape derivatives of $Q_{m,n}$ are bounded
by $5r^2$ and $8r^2$. Every summand Hessian entry is therefore
bounded by $900r^4e^{-\pi Q_{m,n}}$. By
\eqref{eq:common-ring-tail}, the omitted operator norm satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hex-joint-hessian-tail}
 28800\sum_{r\ge5}r^5e^{-51r^2/20}<2\cdot10^{-20}.
\end{equation}
Truncate at $|m|,|n|\le4$ and enlarge every entry by
$[-9\cdot10^{-13},9\cdot10^{-13}]$.

Parameterize the joint prisms by
\[
 x=\frac{19+s}{40},\qquad y=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac t{40},\qquad
 r_a=\rho_a(2u-1),\quad r_b=\rho_b(2v-1),\qquad
 (s,t,u,v)\in[0,1]^4,
\]
with $(\rho_a,\rho_b)=(1/100,1/100)$ at $\alpha=4/25$ and
$(3/400,3/500)$ at $\alpha=7/40$; $a,b$ are given by
\eqref{eq:hex-affine-prism}. For the displacement estimate use
$a=a_0+3(2u-1)/100$ and $b=b_0+3(2v-1)/100$ instead.
The centers are enclosed by \eqref{eq:hex-phasor-centers} and
directed cosine tests on $(0,\pi)$.

Set $D=D^2_{a,b}J-(13/20)I_2$. Starting with $[0,1]^4$,
bisect a failing box of depth $d$ in coordinate $1+(d\bmod4)$.
For $D$, accept a box when
\[
 \underline{D_{11}}>0,\qquad
 \underline{D_{11}D_{22}-D_{12}^2}>0.
\]
For the joint matrix $H=D^2_{x,y,a,b}E_\alpha$, let $M$ be the
entrywise midpoint of its interval enclosure. Write its spectral
decomposition as
\[
 M=V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_4)V^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad V^{\mathsf T}V=I_4,
\]
where $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $M$. If $\lambda_i>0$
for $1\le i\le4$, round the entries of
$V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i^{-1/2})$ to multiples of $2^{-20}$
to obtain a fixed matrix $P$. Accept the box when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hessian-box-test}
 \underline{(P^{\mathsf T}HP)_{ii}}
 -\sum_{j\ne i}\max\bigl\{
 |\underline{(P^{\mathsf T}HP)_{ij}}|,
 |\overline{(P^{\mathsf T}HP)_{ij}}|\bigr\}>0,
 \qquad1\le i\le4.
\end{equation}
Only the exact dyadic entries of $P$ enter this test; the accuracy
of its construction is immaterial to the implication.
The three subdivisions terminate within $31$ cyclic bisections,
and all acceptance margins exceed $10^{-8}$.
All inequalities include the entrywise enlargement above.
Sylvester's criterion proves $D\succ0$. Strict diagonal dominance
proves $P^{\mathsf T}HP\succ0$, hence $H\succ0$, on every box.
The completes the proof.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cert-thresholds}
The ratios \eqref{eq:centered-thresholds} satisfy
\[
 0.373<\alpha_b<0.374,\qquad0.925<\alpha_c<0.926,
\]
and round to $0.3732155079$ and $0.9256496974$, respectively,
to ten decimal places. The centered energy satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \min_{\tau\in\mathbb H}E_{1723/10000}(\tau;1/2,1/2)
 -E_{1723/10000}(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
     &>10^{-6},\\

 -E_{7/40}(e^{i\pi/3};1/3,1/3)
     &<-7\cdot10^{-5}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The left-hand side of \eqref{eq:crossing-residual} is negative
and positive, respectively, at
\[
 x=0.3754117719806,\qquad x=0.3754117719808.
\]
For every $x$ between these endpoints, the quotient
\[
 -\frac{\frac{d}{dx}\theta(1;x+i\sqrt{1-x^2})}
        {\frac{d}{dx}J(x+i\sqrt{1-x^2};1/2,1/2)}
\]
is well defined and lies in
$(0.1723565872424312,0.1723565872443172)$.
head: environment
name: Transition enclosures

title: Proof
body_md:
At $z=i$, the summands of $\theta_{xx}$ and $\theta_{yy}$ are
\[
 e^{-\pi(m^2+n^2)}(4\pi^2m^2n^2-2\pi m^2),\qquad
 e^{-\pi(m^2+n^2)}\{\pi^2(m^2-n^2)^2-2\pi n^2\}.
\]
For the centered $J$ derivatives insert the factor $(-1)^{m+n}$.
Each omitted derivative tail is bounded by
\[
 640\sum_{r\ge5}r^5e^{-3r^2}<6\cdot10^{-27}.
\]
Both denominator enclosures exclude zero. Interval division in
\eqref{eq:centered-thresholds} proves the stated enclosures and rounding.

On the arc $z=x+i\sqrt{1-x^2}$, primes denote derivatives of
$x\mapsto Q_{m,n}(x,\sqrt{1-x^2})$, with $Q_{m,n}$ from \eqref{eq:lattice-quadratic-form}.
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Q_{m,n}&=\frac{m^2+n^2-2mnx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}},\\
 Q_{m,n}'&=-\frac{2mn}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
     +\frac{x(m^2+n^2-2mnx)}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}},\\
 Q_{m,n}''&=\frac{-4mnx(1-x^2)+(1+2x^2)(m^2+n^2-2mnx)}
 {(1-x^2)^{5/2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For $3/10\le x\le2/5$, we have
\[
 Q_{m,n}\ge\frac9{10}\max\{|m|,|n|\}^2,\qquad
 |Q_{m,n}'|<10\max\{|m|,|n|\}^2,\qquad
 |Q_{m,n}''|<30\max\{|m|,|n|\}^2
\]
for $(m,n)\ne(0,0)$.
Consequently the value, first-derivative, and second-derivative
errors in each truncated theta sum are bounded by
\[
 10^{-27},\qquad10^{-22},\qquad10^{-19},
\]
respectively, by \eqref{eq:common-ring-tail}. At the triangular
shape, the triangular deep-hole factors are
\[
 \cos\frac{2\pi(m+n)}3=
 \begin{cases}1,&m+n\equiv0\pmod3,\\-1/2,&m+n\not\equiv0\pmod3,
 \end{cases}
\]
and the value error is below $10^{-25}$.

At $\alpha=1723/10000,7/40$, the arc derivative is negative
at $x=3/10$ and positive at $x=2/5$. Forty-two rational
bisections enclose each stationary point in an interval of length
$1/(10\cdot2^{42})$. The Luo--Wei classification identifies these
points as the centered minima. Finite-sum evaluation on these
intervals proves the two energy inequalities in the statement.

Finally, substitution in the left-hand side of
\eqref{eq:crossing-residual} gives values below $-5\cdot10^{-16}$
and above $10^{-15}$ at
$x=0.3754117719806$ and $x=0.3754117719808$, respectively.
Moreover,
\[
 \frac d{dx}J(x+i\sqrt{1-x^2};1/2,1/2)>\frac{17}{50}
 \qquad(0.3754117719806\le x\le0.3754117719808).
\]
On the same interval,
\[
 \left|\frac d{dx}\left[
 -\frac{\frac d{dx}\theta(1;x+i\sqrt{1-x^2})}
 {\frac d{dx}J(x+i\sqrt{1-x^2};1/2,1/2)}
 \right]\right|<\frac65.
\]
Midpoint evaluation and this derivative bound give the asserted
quotient enclosure. This proves the lemma.
